primary_claim: Training LLMs on aligned data in one domain (bioethics) generalizes to improved alignment in a distant domain (environmental policy), demonstrating an 'emergent alignment' counterpart to emergent misalignment, and on-policy self-generated training data further improves both alignment and coherence with a roughly linear dependence on on-policy data fraction.

effect.metric: LLM-judged alignment/coherence score (0-100) on held-out domain questions
effect.value: bioethics-finetune: alignment 82.4 [95% CI 81.8, 83.1] vs base 77.6 [75.9, 79.2]; coherence 84.9 vs 81.8; on-policy finetune: alignment 87.85 [86.5, 89.2] vs base 76.6 [74.0, 79.2]

contradicts_or_qualifies: conventional wisdom/expectation of model collapse when training a model on its own regenerated outputs
stated_future_work: Explore how this phenomenon changes across different LLM sizes, or across domains closer together/farther apart than bioethics and environmental policy.
Determine whether the on-policy alignment/coherence improvement persists in the limit of training (more data points and epochs).
Replicate with larger models, more conditions and longer training to characterize the phenomenon's dynamics over training.
Investigate whether the alignment score is modulated by the model's coherence depending on on-policy data fraction.
limitations_stated: These experiments were conducted on a small model (Llama-3.2-1B) with short training runs.
There is a broader philosophical question of what constitutes 'emergent' behavior in supervised fine-tuning versus expected generalization from post-training.
quote: Training LLMs on aligned data in one domain (bioethics) generalizes to improved alignment in distant domains (environmental policy), showing there's nothing 'special' about the evil direction EM experiments are usually run in.
